title: test-0131-SOC-HIS-BHAKTI
passage: The Bhakti and Sufi movements brought significant social changes to medieval India by emphasizing personal devotion over rigid rituals. In the South, the Nayanars were devoted to Lord Shiva, while the Alvars were dedicated to Vishnu, both challenging the exclusivity of upper-caste religious control. This spirit of inclusivity continued with the Virashaiva movement, which rejected elaborate temple rituals and advocated for the equality of all, including women. Meanwhile, Sufi masters established centers known as Khanqahs, which served as spiritual retreats for people of all backgrounds to gather and seek guidance. Unlike those who sought political power, figures like Mirabai focused entirely on their deep personal love for the divine, often abandoning worldly status to pursue their faith. Similarly, the teachings of Kabir and Guru Nanak transcended narrow boundaries, as they criticized the empty rituals found in both Hindu and Islamic traditions rather than favoring one over the other. These movements were not about creating new religions or political kingdoms, but about fostering a direct, personal connection with the divine that was accessible to everyone, regardless of their social standing or gender.
